transcript:
# Day 4, Economics and Systems Thinking: Opportunity cost, the one idea economics is built on (named by Friedrich von Wieser, 1914; the idea is much older)

Suppose your bank offers you a chance to lead a new program. It comes with more visibility, a bigger team and a modest raise. You say yes, and the decision feels free, because nobody asked you to give anything up. But something was given up. The evenings you would have spent on the MBA, the other program that will now go to someone else, the quiet year you could have used to recover from the last big push. None of those appear on any invoice. They are the real price.

That is opportunity cost. The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the best alternative you did not take. Not all the alternatives added together, just the single best one. If you spend Saturday studying, the opportunity cost is whatever the most valuable other use of that Saturday would have been, whether that is time with family, a side project or sleep.

The idea sounds obvious once stated, which is exactly why it is dangerous. Our minds price things by what we hand over, usually money, and ignore what we forgo. Economists call the visible price the explicit cost and the forgone alternative the implicit cost. The full cost of anything is both. A free parking space in a crowded city is not free; the land could have been a shop or an apartment. A soldier's time on a base is not free to the nation even if the pay is fixed; that soldier could have been training, resting or doing something else of value.

Here is the example that makes the idea bite. Imagine a business that earns a solid profit on paper. The owner put in a million dollars of her own money and works seventy hours a week. An accountant says she made a hundred thousand dollars this year. An economist asks what the million would have earned sitting in an index fund, and what she could have been paid working seventy hours a week for someone else. If those two together exceed a hundred thousand, the business is losing money in the only sense that matters for the decision of whether to keep running it. The accounting profit is real, but the economic profit, which subtracts opportunity cost, is negative.

The military version is the planner's dilemma. Every battalion committed to one front is a battalion unavailable on another. Every dollar in a ship is a dollar not in aircraft. Good staff work is largely the discipline of writing down the forgone option next to the chosen one.

Now the objection. Critics point out that opportunity cost is often unknowable. You cannot see the road not taken, so you cannot measure it, and people who claim to be reasoning carefully about it are often just dressing up a gut call. There is evidence behind this. Shane Frederick and colleagues found in 2009 that even people trained in economics often neglect opportunity cost unless it is made explicit, and a famous 2005 survey found most professional economists at a conference got a simple textbook opportunity cost question wrong. Defenders of the idea answer that the point was never precision. The point is to ask the question at all. Even a rough estimate of the best alternative beats pretending the alternative does not exist, and the habit of asking "compared to what?" catches a large share of bad decisions before they are made.

This is the first reading in the economics track, and it is first on purpose. Nearly everything that follows is opportunity cost wearing a different coat. Comparative advantage asks who gives up the least to produce something. Thinking at the margin asks what the next unit costs in forgone alternatives. Sunk costs, which you will meet in the game theory track, are the mirror image: money already spent has no opportunity cost anymore, so it should not drive the decision. And in the philosophy track, the Stoics will tell you that attention is the scarcest resource you have, which is a claim about opportunity cost too.

A question for the day: for the biggest commitment on your calendar this week, what is the single best thing you are not doing because of it, and would you still make the trade knowingly?

If you want the primary source, Frederic Bastiat's 1850 essay "That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen" is the oldest clear statement of the idea, and the first section, on the broken window, is only a few pages.
